How Composer applies account context to marketing


Generated by Klaviyo AI


An agency shares five Composer use cases, including side-by-side comparisons with a third-party LLM for analysis, segmentation, form updates, and flow planning. The anecdotal findings highlight how Composer uses Klaviyo account context to identify overlooked details and reduce manual work, alongside its use in migration and sending warm-up planning.


-


**Performance root causes:** Composer identified an opt-in setting change behind an email attribution shift that the third-party LLM missed.


-


**Seasonal audience building:** Composer completed campaign analysis and audience expansion tasks faster in the comparison, offering previews and links to next steps.


-


**Bulk form updates:** Composer updated six BFCM pop-ups while preserving other filters, provided previews, and recommended adding Smart Opt-in.


-


**Connected customer signals:** Composer combined RFM data with email engagement for segmentation and flagged existing-flow conflicts and product returns during flow planning.


-


**Migration warm-up planning:** The agency uses Composer to plan sending warm-ups around audience segments, campaign calendars, and potential higher-click campaigns.

---


My team at[A-Game Digital](https://www.a-game.digital/) , a digital marketing agency focused on lifecycle and retention marketing for B2C brands, uses frontier model LLMs so extensively that we have a Claude Certified Architect on staff. When I first tried[Composer](https://www.klaviyo.com/composer) , Klaviyo’s AI marketing agent, I didn't expect it to match what we were doing in those frontier models.


But I recently gave Composer another try, just to see what it could do. We wanted to see what Composer picks up that a third-party LLM doesn't, so we ran the same prompts side by side.


Here are the 5 Klaviyo Composer use cases that stood out.


## 1. Find the root cause behind two years of campaign performance swings


I asked both Composer and a third-party LLM to analyze two years of campaign data from one account, explain the peaks and valleys in performance, and name possible root causes.


Both came back with similar findings, with one big exception: Composer told me someone had changed the newsletter list from single opt-in to double opt-in. That explained an inflection point in email attribution, since fewer people were getting emails after the change. The third-party LLM didn't catch it.


Because Composer works inside your Klaviyo account, it picks up details like this that a third-party LLM probably won't until it learns what to look for. Composer combines your customer, campaign, flow, and performance data with Klaviyo expertise to help you understand not just what happened, but what to do next. It also shows the sources behind its answers, so you can validate what it finds.


And I’m not the only one seeing these kinds of results. Anna Sophie Fokdal Christensen, head of email and retention at[FABO](https://www.fabo.dk/en) , a holistic ecommerce growth partner for lifestyle and apparel brands, sees a similar value in Composer. “It can connect the analysis with details you might otherwise spend time digging for, giving you a better starting point for deciding what to do next,” she explains.


## 2. Re-engage last year’s BFCM buyers with a new segment


Next, I ran two basic tasks I'd normally do in a third-party LLM:


- Analyze campaign performance.
- Expand audience reach.


The goal was to reach customers who bought during last[Black Friday Cyber Monday](https://www.klaviyo.com/bfcm) (BFCM). They're seasonal buyers, and we wanted to warm them up again.


I ran Composer and the third-party LLM side by side. Composer completed both tasks a lot faster. It knew what to look for and what to ask. And before it did anything, it showed me a preview of what it could create. The third-party LLM didn't do that, and it took slightly longer as it considered the tools available via the[MCP server](https://developers.klaviyo.com/en/docs/klaviyo_mcp_server) and queried data from Klaviyo.


Other AI platforms will tell you they created a segment and ask whether you'd like a campaign next. Composer gives you a hyperlink for the next step. It's a slick way to keep moving, and it does a great job of anticipating what you may want to do next.


## 3. Update 6 BFCM sign-up forms in one pass with Composer


Our next task was updating one brand’s existing BFCM[sign-up forms](https://www.klaviyo.com/blog/top-signup-forms-examples) with a new image, headline, and call to action (CTA). This account had 6 different pop-ups, each triggered by something different, and all of them needed updating.


I asked both AI platforms to clone the existing[pop-ups](https://www.klaviyo.com/blog/ecommerce-email-popup) , create BFCM versions with a holiday image I provided, and use the language I provided. Composer started with one and showed me a preview in the user interface, with the chat alongside it.


While it was working, Composer pointed out that we weren't using[Smart Opt-in](https://help.klaviyo.com/hc/en-us/articles/24743883751451) for text messaging on the pop-up we were focusing on. It recommended adding it. I had no idea why we weren't using it, so I said yes. It catches things like that very well.


Then I tested it. I asked Composer to apply the same changes (headline, behavior, targeting) to the other 5 pop-ups and maintain all their other filters. It gave me links to preview every one. That saved me and my team a lot of time.


Composer uses your brand and business context to make the work it generates more relevant. You direct the outcome and review what it produces, and you retain control over what ultimately goes live.


Brenden Rawson, CEO of[Andzen](https://andzen.co/) , an award-winning CRM lifecycle agency for DTC and ecommerce brands, has Composer “QA everything it touches across forms, emails, and flows, checking desktop and mobile versions, links, alt text, and dynamic product feeds.”


In that way, Rawson says, “bulk updates aren’t the only value. For one client, Composer turned what used to be a 3-hour project into 30 minutes.”


## 4. Build segments and flows that account for RFM group and engagement


On another account, I paired Composer with[Klaviyo Personalization](https://www.klaviyo.com/products/personalization) to improve[segmentation](https://www.klaviyo.com/features/segmentation/strategy) for campaigns. The task combined recency, frequency, and monetary ([RFM](https://www.klaviyo.com/glossary/what-is-rfm-analysis) ) segmentation with engagement metrics.


Let’s say you have a segment of “Current RFM = Needs attention.” You want to see if you can rewarm these customers before the holidays, but determining the ideal cutoff threshold for the days since last purchase or last marketing click is tedious. The default move is to say, "Give me all my champions, my loyal customers, my recent customers, and the ones who need attention."


It takes another round of thinking to say, "Some of those people don't engage with email, so let's find out who they are."


Before Composer, I'd have to work that out manually. With a third-party LLM, I’d have to include explicit instructions to combine purchase behavior with click behavior.


But Composer did it automatically. All I told it was that I wanted to increase reach without hurting deliverability, and that I wanted RFM data to inform the segmentation.


Composer got there much faster than the third-party LLM, and it understood the outcome I wanted better, too. I didn't have to explain that the point was to improve campaign performance, which I might have to do with a third-party LLM.


“Patterns become more useful when you connect the data,” Christensen agrees. “I use Composer to look at RFM alongside email engagement, because neither tells the whole customer story. As with paid media, the absence of a click doesn’t necessarily mean the absence of influence.”


Klaviyo Personalization uses the data already in the B2C CRM to decide who to reach, what to recommend, and when to deliver, across every channel. It keeps RFM groups up to date on every profile, while Audience Optimization drops profiles likely to unsubscribe from campaigns. That lets you include groups like your “Inactive” RFM group without hurting deliverability.


I also ran a side-by-side comparison while designing a next best product flow. Both Composer and the third-party LLM came up with solid approaches for presenting the product, but Composer took it a step further: it warned against colliding with existing flows like browse abandonment, and it accounted for customers who may have returned a product since starting the flow.


## 5. Plan a migration and sending warm-up with Composer


I'm using Composer right now on a migration. As I import segments and work through the steps of planning an account warm-up, I'm giving it the brand's campaign calendar and asking questions like:


- How should we plan these?
- How should we segment the audience for the best warm-up results?
- Are there additional campaigns we could design that suit a warm-up better, with higher click rates?


Composer can run work on a recurring cadence, and you can save your proven prompts, brand standards, or methodologies as custom skills so you don't have to start from scratch every time.


## How Composer compares to a third-party LLM: 3 differences


Note that these impressions are based on my anecdotal experience:


1. **Composer is faster.** Composer isn't limited by API throttling, since it's built into the Klaviyo environment.
2. **Composer is more direct.** When I challenge a third-party LLM on something, like why it built a segment a certain way, it often says something like "Oh yeah, you're right" and changes course. Composer is more direct, with less gray area, and I feel more confident in its answers on the analytical side. This may be because it works directly with the data and makes fewer probabilistic calls.
3. **Composer isn’t expensive for us.** You get a generous amount of free usage up to a certain point, and then you pay. Customers on contract can buy any amount of credits they want.
